subtopic: EXPRESSION OF GOOD WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER PRIOR TO DEPARTURE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subtopic: EXPRESSION OF GOOD WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER PRIOR TO DEPARTURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the house will grant me the indulgence on this, the last opportunity that we will have in this chamber to wish the Prime Minister well when he attends the Commonwealth prime ministers' conference, I would like the opportunity of speaking not only for myself as a former prime minister who knows something of those conferences but I am sure for members in all parts of the house in wishing him well.

subtopic: EXPRESSION OF GOOD WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER PRIOR TO DEPARTURE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: EXPRESSION OF GOOD WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER PRIOR TO DEPARTURE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister will face a conference different from anything he has ever attended before as representatives gather from all parts of the world in a conference representing the greatest number of people dedicated to freedom and peace that has ever occurred in the history of the world. There will be many tremendous problems to be faced. There will be no vote at the conference, but there will finally be a consensus and agreement when men and women, representing every colour and race, sit around that prime ministers' conference table whose desire will be to do their part to assure the preservation of the Commonwealth and the peace of the world.
In that conference the Prime Minister will speak for all Canadians, and I wish him well. It is a challenging, fascinating, tremendous experience, and I am sure when he sees Her Majesty the Queen he will convey to her the loyalty, affection and devotion of Canadians as a whole.
I say again to the Prime Minister, with the great powers he possesses and the challenging opportunities that will be his, that the hopes and aspirations of Canadians will be carried by him. I repeat that he will speak for all Canadians.

subtopic: EXPRESSION OF GOOD WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER PRIOR TO DEPARTURE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: EXPRESSION OF GOOD WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER PRIOR TO DEPARTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues and myself I wish to join the right hon. gentleman in wishing the Prime Minister well. As I am sure he has done, over many years I have watched the development from empire into Commonwealth and have been struck by the most important fact about the present Commonwealth, which is that it is a mixture of forms of government, monarchical and republican, and even more important a mixture of races, every country of every race claiming and having equal status with every other country.
I do not know exactly what the agenda of the Prime Ministers Conference will be, but obviously the question of the treatment of other races in some parts of the Commonwealth, the relationship of the Commonwealth to the United Nations and to events in Europe, the whole problem of feeding a hungry world and of making the Commonwealth work for human equality across the world, are part of the notions that all of us have about the value of the Commonwealth in the present day. And I say without reservation I have confidence that on these matters of human liberty and civil liberty the Prime Minister will represent Canada well, and I wish him an interesting and fruitful time at the conference.

subtopic: EXPRESSION OF GOOD WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER PRIOR TO DEPARTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we, of the Ralliement Creditiste, would like also to wish the Prime Minister a pleasant trip overseas for the conference of the Commonwealth countries. We would also ask him to urge those countries-I have already mentioned that-to put an end to the hostilities in Nigeria and to make representations to England so that it will stop selling arms to Nigeria, in order that peace may be restored in that country where so many people are dying when we are hoping for peace and prosperity everywhere.
We also ask the Prime Minister to suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) that he could relieve his headaches by allowing the Bank of Canada-as some Commonwealth countries are allowing their central banks to do-to grant interest free loans to the provinces and the municipalities to further our country's development.

It is a meeting of men of good will from many lands.

I have not, as I say, been enriched by any previous experience in this regard, but I have taken at least a minimum precaution. I have made sure that I will be occupying the same suite, in the same hotel, that was occupied by the right hon. member for Prince Albert at previous Commonwealth conferences in the hope that perhaps some of his wisdom and knowledge will rub off on me.

I am very conscious of the points underscored by the leader of the New Democratic party, that this is a great occasion for men representing countries of many ethnic and racial origins, situated at varying degrees of the economic and social ladder, to discuss together problems and solutions. I recognize that this is a very important meeting in this sense, that we as equals can discuss problems which make us so unequal because of accidents of birth and geography. I think we can do a great deal to show the world the concepts of pluralism in which we in Canada believe and in which members of the Commonwealth, by the mere fact that they are members of the Commonwealth, also believe.

It can be said that Canada, with its pluralist philosophy does its utmost to direct the Bank of Canada, if not toward the ideology advocated by the hon. member for the Rallie-ment Creditiste, at least toward pluralism where people whatever their origin or their language, can live in peace in a modern world.

subtopic: TORONTO-STATEMENT ON EXPANSION OF FACILITIES
TORONTO-STATEMENT ON EXPANSION OF FACILITIES
speechtext:
While I have the floor, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make an announcement with regard to the Toronto international airport. If copies of this statement have not been circulated to members of the opposition I apologize, and I should like my staff to see that this is done immediately.
In 1966 the Department of Transport engaged a firm of consultants to develop a conceptual plan for expansion of airport facilities to cope with the increases forecast for air line passenger, general aviation and air cargo demands in the Toronto area. The consultant's report submitted to the department in late 1967 concluded that expansion of the present Toronto international airport was the most economic and viable course of action to satisfy these requirements, conditional upon three important factors.
The first was that additional land was available for expansion. The second was that an adequate ground transportation system could be provided; and, third, that land use compatibility could be satisfied with respect to the communities surrounding the airport. After officials of the department had carefully studied the many technical proposals in the report, I announced publicly on August 2 last that the government was prepared to proceed

DEBATES	December 20, 1968
with expansion provided the three conditional matters were met, but it should not be carried out at the expense of the general interest of many residents who live near the airport.
Since the announcement, members of my department and myself from time to time have had a series of meetings with officials of the government of Ontario, with the municipalities surrounding the airport, with interested members of parliament mainly from the Toronto area, with the various members of the air line industry, and with volunteer citizens' groups.
Many citizens of the area expressed concern about the possible increased noise which could be generated by an expanded airport, and a number of the municipalities in the area surrounding the airport said serious problems would be encountered in rearranging existing planning and development programs in adjacent municipalities.
On the basis of the sociological implications of the proposed expansion, and in consideration of the present use of land in the area, the government has concluded that the condition of land use compatibility cannot be satisfied. Consequently we have decided against full scale expansion of the airport at Malton. Instead, a joint federal-provincial government committee will be established to study alternative sites for future expansion to serve the southern Ontario region.
The Toronto international airport will be developed to sufficient capacity to meet presently foreseen requirements for servicing large jets being introduced in 1971, and the volume of passenger traffic up to the late 1970's or even into the early 1980's. The development will include extending an east-west runway in the northern part of the airport, building new terminal facilities, and providing additional service and control facilities to handle the expected increase in passengers and freight. Work will start immediately. The present airport will continue to operate as a base for air carrier operations, for special general aviation operations and as an aircraft industrial base even after a second airport is opened.
Plans for future expansion will take full account of the direction of urban growth in the area. Facilities will provide the most up to date capabilities for dealing with advancing air technology, including supersonic aircraft.
We are satisfied that this alternative proposal can efficiently meet the problem of
December 20, 1968	COMMONS
providing the best in services for the air travelling public, while still protecting the basic rights of the many residents of the Toronto urban area.
There will always be a problem in reconciling the demands of progress with the basic concerns and rights of human beings, and the members of the federal government are fully aware of the difficulties in arriving at solutions satisfactory to everyone. Proper solutions depend upon full co-operation of all members of the community. This proposal for Toronto international airport represents the kind of solution that can emerge when all citizens participate in a dialogue with the government in a spirit of reason and good will.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to table before the house the two versions, English and French of Volume I of the study entitled: "Yukon Economy: Growth and Life Expectation". This volume represents the main part of the survey made by the consulting economists D. William Carr and Associates Limited at the request of the federal and Yukon governments.
It will be recalled, Mr. Speaker, that on September 24, I advised the house that the government had received a preliminary report on this study. Later on, I distributed a summary thereof to the members. At the time, I promised to table the interim report in extenso, as soon as the French version would be ready. However, the consulting economists gave us the final report soon after, and as it was almost identical to the preliminary report, I thought it preferable to table the final report.
The report was handed to us in eight volumes. Volumes 2 to 8 inclusive are studies on documents and will be available for consultation in some of the libraries in Ottawa and Whitehorse.
I should like to point out to the house that the views expressed in this report are not necessarily those of the federal and territorial governments, although those two governments commissioned the study and the report.
The report will be put on sale throughout Canada through the Queen's Printer. Copies have been shipped to the Yukon for immediate sale.

The minister himself has told us it is no secret that there is a conflict between the interest of consumers and the interest of producers. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement to the house on the outcome of the very helpful discussions that have taken place among the representatives of the parties. The course of action that we should like to suggest to the house is that the proposed 16-A provisions be deleted from the fourth report of the special committee, and that thereafter the house be asked to decide today whether or not to adopt the remaining sections of that report, and then the consequential fifth report of the special committee on procedure. We believe that this would meet with approval in all quarters of the house.
To achieve these results I understand that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) is prepared to agree to the withdrawal of his motion for an amendment to the motion for concurrence in the fourth report. A new amendment would then be offered excluding the proposed standing order 16-A from the motion for concurrence. The question on this amendment and on the main motion would be decided today by the house. If the main motion on the fourth report is carried, concurrence in the fifth report would be moved. We have also agreed on the text of a motion to refer the question of the allocation of time to the new standing committee on procedure and organization, and that motion will be put forward for decision today.
The recommendations of the fourth and fifth reports, if adopted by the house, will make major changes in the way this house deals with the business of supply and the examination of public bills. During the course of the debate considerable uneasiness was expressed in various quarters about the suitability of our standing committee system as it now exists to perform the heavy tasks to be assigned to it.
December 20, 1968

Statement on House Leaders' Meeting
For this reason, it has been agreed that after the new standing committee on procedure and organization has been established, in addition to its general reference and the directive to review generally the effects of the various procedural changes, that committee will be given a specific direction to keep under close observation the operation of the standing committees.
The focus of this observation will be concentrated on four points. The first of these will be the way the standing committees are studying the estimates. The second will be the possibility of making the position of standing committee chairmen somewhat more comparable to that of the chairman of the committees of the whole house. The third will be the matter of ministerial attendance at the meetings of the standing committees. The fourth point will be the need to make available stronger and more extensive support facilities of various kinds to the standing committees. As I said, a motion embodying that instruction will be made when the new standing committee on procedure and organization has been established.
Before taking my seat perhaps I can say a few words of appreciation to members on all sides of the house, particularly to my colleagues the house leaders. I think it can be agreed that we are now engaged in an historic change in the rules of the house, but that in the process we have had an historic debate on the subject. I think it can also be agreed generally that the debate has brought forward with greater clarity the principal issues in our parliamentary system.
Equally I do not think there can be any doubt that the result of our deliberations and the strenuous opinions that were shared across the floor will in the long run make for a better and more effective system. Therefore I should like to express my thanks to all hon. members, and especially to those with whom I have had the privilege of conducting these discussions.

I believe we will be able to begin our work in 1969 with a set of rules that will be helpful to us. I should like to join with others who have spoken in thanking those who have helped us.
I appreciate particularly the support and tremendous interest of all members of this party in this whole problem. It has been a pleasure to work with the other house leaders and the members of the committee. It was not always easy to say that. There were one or two nights when it was no pleasure at all. Now that we have resolved the difficulty in a parliamentary fashion it is a pleasure for me to join with others in expressing this work of approval of what we have now accomplished.

subtopic: STATEMENT FOLLOWING DISCUSSION AMONG HOUSE LEADERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my name and on behalf of my colleagues, I am very happy to assure the house that we accept the proposals made by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) about the withdrawal of rule 16A, and we believe that the discussions that took place gave very good results.
We all agree that our procedure must be changed and we believe that all hon. members who took part in the debate these last few days gave their best in order to attain the goal we were all seeking, the streamlining of our parliamentary procedure.
I would also like to congratulate all the members of the committee on procedure, who held 26 sittings, for the wonderful work they did. I hope that the task with which they will be entrusted this afternoon will be carried out satisfactorily and that their work will be as fruitful as anything done until now.

subtopic: STATEMENT FOLLOWING DISCUSSION AMONG HOUSE LEADERS
speechtext:
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: INSTRUCTION TO STANDING COMMITTEE RESPECTING ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
As I indicated in the statement I made on motions, there has been agreement in the house with respect to the reference of the question of the allocation of time to the standing committee on procedure and organization which we just established under the terms of the fifth report.
I would confirm, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) suggested, that the statement which I made was the agreed statement, and equally that the following proposed motion is also the agreed motion. I must say I did not hear all the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition, but I would simply confirm that my understanding of the agreement is as stated in both this motion and in my statement. I take it there is no doubt about the fact that these two documents comprise the agreement between both sides of the house.
On this basis, I move:
That the standing committee on procedure and organization be instructed, and hereby is instructed, to consider and to propose ways to allocate time to the legislative business of the house and to include in its report or reports a draft of a proposed standing order drawn to give effect, if adopted by the house, to the proposal of the committee; and for greater certainty but not to restrict the generality of the foregoing, the committee is instructed to consider the British rules and practice for the allocation of time, the suggestions made by the Leader of the Opposition on December 10, 1968, the suggestions made by the Minister of Agriculture on December 13, 1968, and other proposals and suggestions made in the debate on the motion for concurrence in the fourth report of the special committee on procedure.
Motion agreed to.
